alignment.note: The Peshitta fuses the conjunction and verb in a single inflected form ܘܫܚܪܘ ('and they compelled/pressed into service'), so the Syriac waw-prefix carries both καί and ἀγγαρεύουσιν; the Greek and Latin keep conjunction and verb discrete. Note also that the Greek historic present ἀγγαρεύουσιν is rendered as a perfect/preterite in both Syriac and Latin angariaverunt.

Greek uses the present participle παράγοντά and Latin matches with prætereuntem; the Peshitta expresses the durative idea analytically with ܕܥܒܪ ܗܘܐ ('who was passing by'), pairing the participle/verb with the auxiliary ܗܘܐ, a standard Syriac periphrastic past-continuous construction.
τινα / ܚܕ / quempiam — indefinite 'a certain one'.

Greek ἐρχόμενον and Latin venientem render 'coming' with a single participle, whereas the Peshitta again employs the analytic periphrasis ܕܐܬܐ ܗܘܐ ('who was coming'), with the auxiliary ܗܘܐ marking past continuous aspect — a recurring Syriac stylistic preference rather than a semantic difference.
τὸν πατέρα / ܐܒܘܗܝ / patrem — 'the father'; the Syriac encodes the article and possessive within the bound suffixed form ܐܒܘܗܝ ('his father').

Greek ἀγροῦ ('field, country') and Latin villa ('farmstead, country estate') denote agricultural land outside the city; the Peshitta reads ܩܪܝܬܐ ('village, hamlet'), a slight semantic shift from open countryside toward an inhabited rural settlement, reflecting the translator's contextualisation of ἀγρός as a populated locality.

Greek καὶ Ῥούφου and Latin et Rufi coordinate with a separate conjunction; the Peshitta ܘܕܪܘܦܘܣ fuses the coordinating waw and the genitive/dependency marker d- into a single prefixed cluster on the proper name, an economy of Syriac morphology rather than a textual divergence.
ἵνα / d- (in ܕܢܫܩܘܠ) / ut — purpose clause marker.

Greek ἄρῃ ('lift, carry') and Latin tolleret ('take up, carry') belong to the same general 'bear' semantic field; the Peshitta uses ܫܩܠ (root sh-q-l, 'to take up, raise, bear'), cognate with Hebrew שָׁקַל, an apt lexical equivalent though from a distinct etymological stock.

Greek σταυρόν and Latin crucem use the standard 'cross' lexeme; the Peshitta ܙܩܝܦܗ derives from the root z-q-p ('to raise, set upright, crucify'), the characteristic Syriac term for the instrument of crucifixion, with the article and pronominal 'his' (αὐτοῦ / ejus) bound as the suffix -eh.
